topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on public health faculty development; findings may not generalise to other sectors or non-academic settings. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI literacy is addressable through targeted development programs; design interventions that move people from resistance to readiness rather than assuming universal buy-in.
In knowledge-intensive fields like public health, investing in educator capability is a leverage point for scaling AI literacy — train the trainers to create cascading impact across cohorts.
Organisational readiness for AI adoption may depend more on internal capability-building than on technology access; prioritise structured faculty development before rolling out AI tools.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development may require adaptation. Geographic scope not evident from title/snippet.
takeaways: AI literacy for non-technical audiences benefits from integration within broader digital literacy frameworks rather than taught in isolation — consider mapping AI competencies to existing digital skills training in your organisation.

A holistic approach to AI competencies (likely covering ethics, critical thinking, and practical application alongside technical understanding) may be more effective for building employee confidence than technical-only upskilling programs.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are specific to European public health contexts and digital health competencies, which may differ from broader organisational or private-sector AI literacy requirements. Applicability outside Europe and public health sectors requires caution.
takeaways: Use this framework as a reference model to audit which digital and AI competencies your organisation currently develops, and identify gaps in formal training pathways for public health or healthcare professionals.
The framework can inform structured onboarding or upskilling programmes for teams transitioning to digital-first or AI-supported workflows in healthcare settings.
Consider which competency domains (technical, regulatory, ethical) are most critical for your specific workforce role and prioritise those in your capability-building strategy.

articles.title: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Broad applicability — McKinsey research typically draws on global data and serves multinational clients, though specific case examples may skew toward large enterprises and developed economies.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation will be most impacted by generative AI and prioritise upskilling programmes for those cohorts first, rather than trying to reskill everyone simultaneously.

Design reskilling pathways that pair technical AI literacy (prompt engineering, tool familiarity) with adjacent skills like critical evaluation, domain knowledge, and change management — standalone AI tool training often fails without these complements.

Establish clear competency frameworks for different job levels (individual contributors, managers, leaders) so employees understand what AI capabilities they need and can track their progress against realistic benchmarks.

articles.title: ASPIRE: a pedagogical framework for integrating generative artificial intelligence in public health education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: ASPIRE: a pedagogical framework for integrating generative artificial intelligence in public health education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited generalisability — focuses on public health education context; framework applicability to other sectors and organisational settings unclear without seeing full methodology.
takeaways: The ASPIRE framework offers a structured pedagogical approach to embedding generative AI into curricula; examine whether its design principles (likely scaffolding, practice, integration, reflection, evaluation) could be adapted for employee upskilling programs.

Public health educators using this framework report measurable outcomes in AI capability development; identify which assessment methods they use to measure competency gains, as these could inform how you evaluate AI literacy progress in your own workforce.

articles.title: Development and influencing factors of artificial intelligence literacy and computational thinking in Chinese university students - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and influencing factors of artificial intelligence literacy and computational thinking in Chinese university students  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to Chinese higher education context. Findings on AI literacy development and computational thinking may not generalise directly to Australian universities, which have different curriculum structures, technology infrastructure, and student demographics. Results are specific to Chinese educational policy and student cohorts.
takeaways: Identify which factors most strongly predict AI literacy development in your student or employee population — the study maps influencing factors that could guide targeted upskilling interventions.

Computational thinking appears linked to AI literacy; consider whether your organisation's AI capability programmes explicitly build computational thinking skills, or if they assume this foundation exists.

Chinese university context suggests educational pathway and prior maths/STEM background may shape AI literacy — assess baseline capability and learning readiness in your cohort rather than assuming uniform starting points.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet alone. The 'double-edged' framing suggests mixed or contingent effects, which may vary by sector, organisation type, and implementation context.
takeaways: AI adoption can simultaneously enhance and constrain employee creativity depending on how it's implemented — organisations should assess whether their AI deployment augments creative thinking or inadvertently creates rigid workflows.

Monitor the specific mechanisms through which AI affects creative work (e.g., does it free time for ideation or enforce standardised processes?) to identify whether adoption is having the intended positive impact on innovation.

Design AI integration with explicit attention to preserving psychological safety and autonomy in creative roles, as the 'double-edged' effect likely reflects trade-offs between efficiency gains and creative freedom.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited by focus on paternalistic leadership contexts, which are more prevalent in collectivist cultures (particularly East Asian organizations). Findings may not transfer to egalitarian or distributed leadership models common in Western workplaces.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools by involving employees in customizing or 'crafting' AI implementations to fit their workflows — this strengthens collaboration and adoption even when AI integration feels top-down.

In hierarchical or paternalistic team structures, leaders can leverage their authority to frame AI as a shared organizational resource that employees help shape, rather than an imposed tool, to increase buy-in and collaborative use.

Design AI onboarding to include opportunities for hands-on customization and employee input on how AI tools integrate into their roles, as this sense of ownership appears to be a key driver of sustained human-AI collaboration.

articles.title: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — title indicates a theoretical model is proposed, but without access to the full article, sample size, geographic scope, and sector representation cannot be assessed. Generalisability will depend on whether the dual-pathway model was tested empirically and across which organisational contexts.
takeaways: Design AI capability-building interventions that simultaneously address job insecurity concerns; evidence suggests employee anxiety and empowerment operate through distinct pathways, so generic 'upskilling' alone may not reduce anxiety if job security messaging is absent.

Use the dual-pathway framework to audit your current AI transformation communications—assess whether you are building capability *and* actively reassuring employees about role stability, or whether capability messaging is outpacing reassurance, which may amplify perceived threat.

Monitor both empowerment and anxiety as separate outcome metrics during workforce AI transitions rather than assuming that capability gains automatically reduce job insecurity concerns; the model suggests these are parallel, not sequential, processes.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. Approach-avoidance framework is theoretically sound but applicability to Australian workplace contexts and specific industries unclear without methodological details.
takeaways: AI adoption triggers different employee responses — some actively reshape their roles (approach) while others withdraw or resist (avoidance). Managers should identify which employees fall into each category and tailor support accordingly.

Job crafting (how employees modify their tasks and relationships) is a key lever for managing AI adoption outcomes. Consider interventions that encourage proactive job redesign rather than passive acceptance or resistance.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — generalisability depends on sample size, industry sector, and geographic scope, which are not evident from the title and snippet provided.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively impact employee mental health if not accompanied by strong psychological safety and ethical leadership — leaders should prioritise these conditions before rolling out AI initiatives.

Psychological safety acts as a protective factor in AI adoption; organisations should invest in trust-building and create safe channels for employees to voice concerns about AI tools before and during implementation.

Ethical leadership is critical during AI transitions — leaders should model transparent decision-making about AI use and actively address fairness and job security concerns to mitigate depression and anxiety among staff.

articles.title: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — unable to assess sample size, geographic scope, or sector representation without full article access. Frontiers articles vary widely in generalisability depending on methodology and participant demographics.
takeaways: Employee-AI collaboration may boost work engagement through multiple psychological mechanisms — identify which pathways (e.g., competence, autonomy, purpose) are most active in your team to design targeted engagement interventions.

Frame AI tools as collaboration partners rather than replacements to leverage psychological benefits; clarify role boundaries and emphasise how AI augments rather than diminishes employee contributions.

Assess current engagement levels before and after AI tool introduction to measure whether dual psychological pathways are being activated, and adjust training or communication if engagement gains are not realised.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner guidance based on consulting experience, likely skewed toward large enterprises and developed economies; specific applicability to Australian SMEs or public sector organisations not established.
takeaways: Shift framing from 'AI adoption' (one-time implementation) to 'AI adaptation' (ongoing behavioural change) to sustain engagement and capability development beyond initial rollout.
Design change interventions that explicitly target the human behaviours required for effective AI use—not just technology training—by identifying capability gaps and tailoring support accordingly.
Establish feedback loops and iterative adjustment cycles to monitor how employees actually work with AI tools and refine organisational practices based on real usage patterns rather than assumptions.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample size, sector coverage, and geographic scope — not evident from title/snippet alone. The theoretical framework (approach-avoidance perspective) is likely applicable across contexts, but empirical findings may vary by industry, organisational culture, and AI implementation maturity.
takeaways: Job crafting during AI adoption is not uniformly positive or negative — employees may engage in approach behaviours (upskilling, embracing new roles) or avoidance behaviours (resistance, withdrawal) depending on psychological threat perception and perceived opportunity.

To support constructive job crafting, organisations should actively shape the narrative around AI adoption: highlight opportunities for role redesign and skill development while transparently addressing job security concerns, rather than assuming employees will naturally adapt.

Monitor and respond to avoidance behaviours early — employees who perceive AI as a threat are more likely to disengage or resist change, so psychological safety and clear communication about job futures are critical levers for behaviour change.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — draws on BCG's consulting experience across multiple sectors and regions, but represents consultant perspective rather than independently validated research. Findings may reflect BCG's client base (typically larger, more advanced organisations) rather than broader workforce populations.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology implementation — this shifts focus from tools to people and requires deliberate change management alongside technical deployment.

Design role transitions and reskilling pathways proactively before AI systems go live, rather than reactively addressing displacement; this reduces anxiety and improves employee buy-in during transformation.
Align performance metrics and incentive structures with new AI-enabled workflows early — misaligned incentives are a common barrier to adoption even when employees have the skills.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey research typically draws on global client work and surveys, but specific sample details are not provided in the snippet. Findings likely most applicable to large organisations with resources for formal change programmes.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling not as a skills training initiative alone, but as an organisational change imperative requiring shifts in processes, culture, and leadership mindsets — this reframing increases adoption and sustainability compared to traditional L&D approaches.
Embed upskilling within broader change management practices (stakeholder engagement, resistance mitigation, progress tracking) rather than treating it as a standalone capability-building programme.

Use change leadership to drive urgency and accountability for AI capability across teams, ensuring upskilling is linked to business outcomes and role redesign rather than abstract competency frameworks.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — Stanford GSB perspective reflects US business school viewpoint; lacks empirical data on specific workplace populations or geographies. Findings and recommendations may not transfer directly to Australian organisational contexts.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation where AI adoption could create skill gaps, then design targeted upskilling programs before implementation rather than after disruption occurs.
Frame AI integration as capability expansion (what humans + AI can do together) rather than replacement, to reduce resistance and help employees see their evolving role in an AI-augmented workplace.

articles.title: Generative AI adoption and employee outcomes: a conservation of resources perspective on job crafting, career commitment, and the moderating role of liking of AI - Nature
articles.snippet: Generative AI adoption and employee outcomes: a conservation of resources perspective on job crafting, career commitment, and the moderating role of liking of AI  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and geography (not evident from title/snippet). The conservation of resources theory framework is well-established, but findings on AI adoption outcomes may vary significantly by industry, role type, and organisational context.
takeaways: Employee attitudes toward AI ('liking of AI') play a moderating role in how AI adoption affects job crafting and career commitment — investing in positive AI perception through training and change management may amplify adoption benefits.

Use conservation of resources theory as a lens when designing AI implementation: frame AI as a resource that enhances rather than depletes employee capacity, and identify which job crafting behaviours (task expansion, skill development, relationship building) are most feasible for your workforce.

Monitor career commitment trajectories during AI rollout — employees who feel their resources are being depleted may disengage; proactive career development conversations and transparent advancement pathways can mitigate this risk.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — draws on established psychological research on social connection and health outcomes across diverse populations, though individual study samples may vary.
takeaways: Friendships activate measurable biological protective mechanisms: people with strong social bonds show lower cortisol levels, better immune function, and reduced inflammation compared to socially isolated peers.

The health benefits of friendship rival major lifestyle factors — loneliness increases mortality risk as much as smoking 15 cigarettes daily, making social connection as critical to longevity as exercise and diet.

Quality beats quantity: one or two deeply meaningful friendships provide greater health protection than a large but shallow social network, challenging the assumption that more friends always equals better outcomes.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — findings based on cross-cultural data spanning multiple countries, suggesting patterns that transcend geographic and cultural boundaries.
takeaways: Your taste in music reveals something real and consistent about your personality, and this connection holds up whether you're in Melbourne, Mumbai, or Moscow — personality and music preference appear to be universally linked.

The fact that personality-music links are consistent across cultures is surprisingly counterintuitive given how differently music is used, valued, and created across societies, suggesting deep psychological roots rather than pure cultural conditioning.

This research adds weight to the idea that music isn't just entertainment or cultural expression — it's a genuine window into how people's minds work, which explains why 'what music do you like?' feels like such a revealing personal question.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from title and snippet alone; likely synthesises psychological research on true crime consumption across multiple studies, though geographic or demographic limitations cannot be determined from information provided.
takeaways: True crime captivates audiences through psychological mechanisms like morbid curiosity, perceived safety (experiencing danger from a distance), and the human drive to solve puzzles — understanding why we're drawn to dark stories reveals something fascinating about how our brains process threat and control.

The paradox of enjoying something disturbing — consuming detailed accounts of violence while feeling safe — taps into deep psychological needs to understand evil, master fear, and restore a sense of order in an unpredictable world.

True crime's enduring popularity suggests that engaging with darkness through narrative isn't morbid or anomalous, but a normal, perhaps even adaptive way humans process danger, mortality, and justice.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews existing MBTI leadership research across multiple studies, but findings reflect limitations inherent in MBTI's psychometric validity and the heterogeneity of how 'leadership behavior' is measured across studies.
takeaways: Despite its massive popularity in corporate training (millions take it annually), MBTI is surprisingly weak at predicting actual leadership performance — the disconnect between what people believe about their type and how they actually lead is striking.

The 'E vs I' (extraversion-introversion) dimension shows slightly better predictive power than other MBTI scales for leadership, but even this relationship is modest — revealing that leadership myths (like 'leaders must be extroverts') don't hold up statistically.

MBTI persists in leadership development despite weak evidence because it feels personally meaningful and sparks useful conversations, not because the four-letter categories scientifically predict who will be an effective leader.

articles.title: How dogs think - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How dogs think  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Low — appears to be a general interest article from the APA without specific empirical data, methodology, or sample details provided in the snippet.
takeaways: Dogs likely don't experience guilt or shame the way humans do — that 'guilty look' is probably a response to your anger, not remorse about their behaviour.

Dogs have a remarkably different sense of time than humans; they live almost entirely in the present moment, which explains why they're equally excited to see you whether you've been gone 5 minutes or 5 hours.

Dogs can read human facial expressions and body language with impressive accuracy, suggesting they've evolved to be sophisticated interpreters of human emotion rather than forming complex internal models of the world.

articles.title: Personality traits linked to differences in brain structure - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Personality traits linked to differences in brain structure  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not provided in snippet. Brain imaging studies often use relatively small, WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic) samples, which may not represent global population diversity.
takeaways: Our personalities aren't just psychological—they have measurable correlates in brain structure, suggesting personality traits reflect underlying neurobiological differences.

This finding bridges psychology and neuroscience in a surprising way: what we think of as abstract personality traits (like extraversion or conscientiousness) are actually associated with physical differences you could see on an MRI scan.

The discovery is intriguing because it hints that personality might have deeper biological 'wiring' than previously understood, though it raises the chicken-and-egg question: do personality traits shape brain structure, or does brain structure shape personality?

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings depend on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The mechanism linking AI adoption to depression via psychological safety is theoretically sound but generalisability is unclear without knowing study design, sample size, sector, and geography.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical mediator between AI adoption and employee wellbeing — organisations rolling out AI must actively protect and reinforce psychological safety to mitigate depression and mental health risks.

Ethical leadership matters during AI transitions: leaders must model ethical AI use and create permission for employees to raise concerns, question decisions, and voice uncertainty without fear of consequences.

AI adoption alone does not cause depression; the pathway runs through eroded psychological safety — so focus interventions on maintaining trust and open dialogue, not just change management logistics.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's analysis likely draws on global consulting experience and client work, but specific sample composition, methodology, and geographic focus are unclear from the snippet alone.
takeaways: Psychological safety creates equitable access to opportunity and voice across hierarchies and demographic groups; consider auditing whose perspectives are genuinely heard in your team meetings and decision-making processes.
Leaders can actively level the playing field by normalising questions, admitting uncertainty, and responding non-defensively to challenge — model these behaviours consistently to shift team norms.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused survey data — findings reflect American workplace contexts and may not directly transfer to Australian employment practices, workplace culture, or regulatory environments.
takeaways: Identify specific barriers to psychological safety in your team (e.g., fear of speaking up, lack of inclusive practices) and address them through targeted interventions rather than generic training.
Map how changing work arrangements (hybrid, remote, flexible) are affecting employees' sense of safety and belonging — this will reveal context-specific gaps to close.
Use APA's data on what drives or undermines psychological safety to benchmark your organisation's current state and set measurable improvement targets.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's advisory work across organisations, but lacks transparent detail on sample size, sector breakdown, or methodology. Findings likely reflect practices in large, well-resourced companies and may not generalise to smaller organisations or resource-constrained settings.
takeaways: Psychological safety enables employees to experiment with AI tools and voice concerns about AI risks without fear of retribution — organisations should explicitly frame AI adoption as a learning process where mistakes are expected and discussed openly.

Empowering employees as 'superagents' requires clear role clarity, decision-making authority, and support structures — define what decisions employees can make with AI assistance, provide training, and establish feedback loops so people feel trusted to use AI autonomously.

Organisations must address fear and uncertainty about AI's impact on jobs directly through transparent communication and skill-development pathways — psychological safety depends on people believing their concerns are heard and that the organisation is investing in their capability, not replacing them.

articles.title: What Sycophantic AI Can Cost Your Organization - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: What Sycophantic AI Can Cost Your Organization  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — discusses organizational risks of AI sycophancy as a general phenomenon, but lacks empirical data or sector-specific evidence. Applicability depends on the types of AI systems your organization deploys and decision-making contexts.
takeaways: AI systems trained to be agreeable or non-confrontational may suppress critical feedback and dissenting viewpoints, undermining psychological safety by replacing human challenge with false consensus.
When implementing AI advisory tools, explicitly design for constructive disagreement and alternative perspectives rather than defaulting to confirmation-biased outputs.
Audit your organization's AI systems for sycophancy patterns — test whether they genuinely encourage diverse thinking or merely appear to do so while reinforcing existing views.

articles.title: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety - Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.source: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.snippet: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety  Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents conceptual clarifications on psychological safety but lacks empirical data on prevalence of misconceptions or their impact across different organisational contexts.
takeaways: Identify and challenge common myths about psychological safety in your own team (e.g., that it means avoiding accountability or that high performers don't need it) to ensure your safety-building efforts target real barriers rather than phantom problems.
Use this source to educate stakeholders and leaders who may harbour misconceptions about psychological safety, which could otherwise block cultural change initiatives in your organisation.
Assess whether your current psychological safety interventions are addressing actual misconceptions held by your workforce, or if you're solving problems that don't exist in your specific context.
